questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply data leakage to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Taking data leakage instance 1801, a practitioner computes feature means and scaling parameters over the entire labeled dataset, and only afterward splits the data into training and test sets, then reports an unusually high test accuracy. What is the most likely flaw in this procedure? Work through it carefully, showing the key step.

options.text: Overfitting from too few training epochs.
options.misconception: Wrongly attributes the issue to training duration.

options.text: Class imbalance: one label dominates the dataset.
options.misconception: Wrongly diagnoses label skew, which is not described.

options.text: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the task.
options.misconception: Wrongly blames model capacity instead of information flow.

options.text: Leakage: test-set statistics influenced the training pipeline.

questions.explanation: Because the scaling statistics were computed before the split, information from the test set leaked into the transformation applied during training. This data leakage inflates test performance because the held-out examples influenced preprocessing. The other options name unrelated problems: model capacity, label distribution, and training duration are not implicated by preprocessing on the full dataset.
questions.hint: Ask whether any test-set information entered the pipeline before the split.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply decision thresholds to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Taking decision thresholds instance 1802, a probabilistic classifier outputs a score for the positive class. If the decision threshold for predicting positive is raised while the model and data stay fixed, what generally happens to recall and precision? Work through it carefully, showing the key step.

options.text: Neither metric changes with the threshold.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes threshold and metrics are independent.

options.text: Recall rises while precision tends to fall.
options.misconception: Describes the effect of lowering, not raising, the threshold.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

options.text: Recall falls while precision tends to rise.

questions.explanation: Raising the threshold makes positive predictions harder to earn, so fewer true positives are captured and recall falls. The predictions that remain positive are on average more confident, so precision tends to rise. Lowering the threshold produces the opposite pattern, and the two metrics do trade off, so they cannot both move together or stay fixed in general.
questions.hint: Consider which predictions are relabeled when the cutoff moves upward.

questions.learningObjective: Apply intelligent agents to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: With the data 9 / 2 / 3 in view, a performance measure awards +9 points for each correctly filed document, subtracts 2 for each misfiled document, and subtracts 3 for each second of delay. An agent files 7 documents correctly, misfiles 3, and finishes in 3 seconds. What total score does the performance measure assign to this behavior?

options.misconception: Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it
Counts misplaced items as if they were correctly sorted
Treats delay cost as a reward instead of a penalty

questions.explanation: The measure sums three signed contributions: +9 times 7 correctly filed documents gives 63, minus 2 times 3 misfiles gives -6, and minus 3 times 3 seconds gives -9. The total 63 - 6 - 9 = 48 rewards correctness and penalizes both errors and delay. Adding the delay term, adding the misfiles, or crediting misfiles as correct all invert the intended penalties, so those totals are wrong.
questions.hint: Write each contribution with its sign, then add the three products.

questions.learningObjective: Apply problem formulation to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: In the small toy dataset below, a classifier produces the following output. Reviewing problem formulation: a cleaning robot maps a room but cannot observe furniture that family members move after it looks away. Its wheel commands have perfectly predictable effects, yet the room layout keeps changing while it works and positions vary over a continuum. Which set of environment properties best characterizes this task? Work through it carefully, and state the conclusion.

options.text: Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.
options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, static, discrete.
options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Fully observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.
options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.

questions.explanation: The robot cannot see every relevant fact, so the environment is partially observable. Actions have perfectly predictable effects, so it is deterministic. The layout changes while the agent deliberates, so it is dynamic. Positions range over a continuum, so it is continuous. Each competing option flips one of these four properties and therefore misdescribes the task.
questions.hint: Check observability, action predictability, change over time, and whether the state space is discrete.

questions.stem: In the small toy dataset below, a classifier returns the reported scores. Reviewing agent designs: an agent selects each action using only the percept it receives at this instant. options.misconception: Wrongly assumes explicit goals and lookahead search.

options.text: A utility-based agent maximizing expected satisfaction.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes a utility function over outcomes.

options.text: A model-based reflex agent tracking hidden state.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the agent maintains any state at all.

options.text: A simple reflex agent acting only on the current percept.

questions.explanation: A simple reflex agent maps the current percept directly to an action through condition-action rules, with no memory or world model. The description explicitly denies stored history and an environment model, ruling out model-based, goal-based, and utility-based designs, each of which needs internal state beyond the present percept.

questions.stem: Building on 0 and 9, then 1, on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (9, 9). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state? Give the exact answer.

options.misconception: Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement
Undercounts by assuming the goal square needs no move

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |9 - 0| + |9 - 0| = 9 + 9 = 18. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.
questions.hint: Sum the horizontal and vertical separations independently.

questions.learningObjective: Apply adversarial search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Building on 6 and 7, then 5, a two-ply game tree has a MAX root with two MIN children. The first MIN child has leaves 6 and 7; the second MIN child has leaves 6 and 5. Under minimax with both players choosing optimally, what value is backed up to the root?

options.misconception: Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Assumes MIN chooses at the root
Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 6 and 5. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 6. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.
questions.hint: Evaluate the bottom MIN nodes first, then let the root MAX choose between them.

questions.subject: AI_ML
questions.learningObjective: Apply informed search to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: An instance of informed search, no. 1808: a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Work through it carefully, and state the conclusion.

options.text: Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.text: Optimal: it guarantees the best path without any search.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

options.text: Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

questions.explanation: The inequality h(n) <= h*(n) is exactly the definition of admissibility: the estimate never overestimates the remaining cost. Consistency is a stronger condition involving arc costs between neighboring states, and a heuristic being admissible does not by itself make search instantaneous or optimal without the surrounding algorithm guarantees. The competing options name different or invented properties.
questions.hint: Compare the estimate to the true remaining cost, not to neighbor costs.

questions.learningObjective: Apply bayesian inference to a concrete artificial-intelligence scenario.
questions.stem: Read 0.13 and 0.89 with 0.86 first: a disease has prevalence 0.13. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.89 when present and has specificity 0.86 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

options.misconception: Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized
Reports sensitivity and ignores the base rate

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(D|+) = se*p / (se*p + (1 - sp)*(1 - p)) = 0.116 / (0.116 + 0.122) = 0.4872. The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.
questions.hint: Compute true positives and false positives over a population, then take the true-positive share.

questions.stem: Suppose the values are 0.5, 0.6, and 0.4; in a Bayesian network with edge A -> B, the prior is P(A) = 0.5. The conditional table gives P(B | A) = 0.6 and P(B | not A) = 0.4. What is the joint probability P(A and B), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Reports the conditional probability and ignores the parent
Uses the conditional probability of the wrong parent state

questions.explanation: The joint distribution factorizes as P(A, B) = P(A) * P(B | A) = 0.5 * 0.6 = 0.3. Adding the contribution from not A computes the marginal P(B), and using P(B | not A) or the conditional alone does not follow the factorization for the event A and B together.
questions.hint: Multiply the parent's prior by the child's conditional given that parent state.

questions.stem: Considering propositional logic, case 1811 — given the truth assignment P = true, Q = true, R = true, evaluate the propositional formula (P and Q) or (not P and R). Which statement is correct? Give the exact answer, precisely.

options.text: True, but only when R is false.
options.misconception: Wrongly ties the value to R rather than to the disjuncts.

options.text: Undetermined without knowing Q and R together.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims the truth value cannot be evaluated.

options.text: False, because neither disjunct holds.
options.misconception: Reverses the truth value of the disjunction.

options.text: True, because at least one disjunct holds.

questions.explanation: With P = true and Q = true, the first conjunct P and Q is true. With not P = false and R = true, the second conjunct is false. The disjunction of true and false is true, so at least one disjunct holds. The alternatives either invert the result or wrongly claim the value is undecidable when all atoms are assigned.
questions.hint: Evaluate each conjunction first, then combine them with or.

Given the figures 6, 2, 0.2, for the loss L(w) = (w - 6)^2, gradient descent uses learning rate 0.2 from starting weight w = 6. The derivative is dL/dw = 2(w - 6). What is the weight after one update step, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

options.misconception: Drops the factor of two from the derivative
Ignores the learning rate entirely
Performs gradient ascent by flipping the update sign

questions.explanation: The gradient at w = 6 is 2(6 - 6) = 0. The descent update is w - lr * grad = 6 - 0.2 * (0) = 6. Adding the gradient instead ascends the loss, dropping the factor of two uses the wrong derivative, and omitting the learning rate takes a full-size step, so each alternative is a distinct calculus or step-size error.

questions.stem: A regressor predicts 6, 7, 6 for three examples whose true targets are 5, 5, 9. What is the mean squared error of these predictions, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Forgets to divide by the number of examples
Corrupts the first residual by adding instead of subtracting
Uses mean absolute error instead of squared error

questions.explanation: The squared residuals are (6 - 5)^2, (7 - 5)^2, and (6 - 9)^2, summing to 14. Dividing by the three examples gives 4.6667. Mean absolute error squares nothing, skipping the division reports the total rather than the mean, and adding in any residual uses the wrong sign, so those values are not the MSE.
questions.hint: Square each prediction-minus-target residual, add them, then divide by three.

questions.stem: A classifier's confusion matrix reports 30 true positives, 9 false positives, and 7 false negatives. What is the F1 score for the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Reports recall and ignores precision
Uses a simplified accuracy that drops true negatives
Reports precision and ignores recall

questions.explanation: Precision is 30/(30+9) = 0.7692 and recall is 30/(30+7) = 0.8108. The F1 score is their harmonic mean 2PR/(P+R) = 0.7895. Reporting precision or recall alone captures only one side of the tradeoff, and the simplified ratio is neither a harmonic mean nor the full accuracy.
questions.hint: Compute precision and recall, then take their harmonic mean.

questions.stem: From the inputs 4, 5, 3, a linear regression model predicts with weights 4 and 5, and intercept 4. For an input with feature values x = 3 and y = 3, what value does the model predict?

options.misconception: Subtracts the intercept instead of adding it
Multiplies the features instead of weighting them
Omits the intercept term from the prediction

questions.explanation: A linear model computes the weighted sum plus the intercept: 4*3 + 5*3 + 4 = 12 + 15 + 4 = 31. Dropping the intercept, reversing its sign, or multiplying the features together all change the affine form that defines linear regression.

questions.stem: In the small toy dataset below, a classifier gives the following estimate. A logistic regression model computes a logit of z = -5 for a given input. What is the predicted probability of the positive class, to four decimals? Give the exact answer, based on the details given.

Reports the complement probability of the positive class
Flips the exponent sign, inverting the sigmoid

questions.explanation: The sigmoid maps a logit z to 1/(1 + e^{-z}) = 1/(1 + e^{--5}) = 0.0067. Reversing the exponent sign gives the complement, the linear-ratio substitute is not the logistic function, and reporting 1 minus the probability gives the negative-class probability. Only the sigmoid transformation is correct.

questions.stem: From the inputs 0.6, 0.7, 0.3, a naive Bayes classifier has class prior 0.6. Given two observed features, the class-conditional likelihoods for the positive class are 0.7 and 0.6, and for the negative class they are 0.3 and 0.3. What is the posterior probability of the positive class, to four decimals?

options.misconception: Uses a single likelihood and ignores the other evidence
Reports the prior and ignores the observed features
Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior

questions.explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies likelihoods under the conditional-independence assumption: the positive score is 0.6*0.7*0.6 = 0.252 and the negative score is (1-0.6)*0.3*0.3 = 0.036. questions.hint: Multiply each class's prior by its likelihoods, then normalize across classes.

questions.stem: In the small toy dataset below, a classifier computes this result. A decision-tree leaf contains 9 examples of one class and 9 of the other. What is the Gini impurity of this leaf, to four decimals? Give the exact answer.

Computes entropy instead of Gini impurity
Reports purity, the complement of Gini impurity

Reports half the margin, forgetting the factor of two

questions.stem: The numbers 7 and 6 with 0.95 apply here; in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 7 and leads to state s'. From s' the best action has Q-value 7 (the two successor Q-values are 7 and 6), and the discount factor is gamma = 0.95. What is the target value r + gamma * max Q(s', a'), to four decimals?

options.misconception: Forgets to discount the future value
Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum
Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum

questions.explanation: The one-step target is r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') = 7 + 0.95 * 7 = 13.65. Using one successor value ignores the maximization, dropping the discount fails to reduce future rewards, and summing successors double-counts the future. The Bellman optimality target requires exactly the maximum of the successor values.
questions.hint: Take the largest successor Q-value, discount it, and add the immediate reward.

Discounts the immediate reward as well
Sums rewards with no discounting

questions.explanation: The discounted return weights each reward by gamma raised to its time index: 6 + 0.8*6 + 0.8^2*5 = 14. Summing without discount treats future rewards as equal to immediate ones, dropping the last term truncates the horizon, and applying gamma to the first reward discounts the immediate reward, which the definition does not do.

Omits the logarithm in the idf factor
Uses a base-ten logarithm instead of the natural logarithm

What is the most likely flaw in this procedure? Work through it carefully, and state the conclusion.

options.misconception: Wrongly diagnoses label skew, which is not described.

options.text: Overfitting from too few training epochs.
options.misconception: Wrongly attributes the issue to training duration.

options.text: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the task.
options.misconception: Wrongly blames model capacity instead of information flow.

options.text: Leakage: test-set statistics influenced the training pipeline.

questions.stem: A decision thresholds item, number 1836: a probabilistic classifier outputs a score for the positive class. options.text: Recall rises while precision tends to fall.
options.misconception: Describes the effect of lowering, not raising, the threshold.

options.text: Neither metric changes with the threshold.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes threshold and metrics are independent.

options.text: Both precision and recall rise together.
options.misconception: Wrongly assumes the two metrics move in the same direction.

options.text: Recall falls while precision tends to rise.

An agent files 3 documents correctly, misfiles 1, and finishes in 2 seconds. What total score does the performance measure assign to this behavior?

Adds the misplacement penalty rather than subtracting it
Counts misplaced items as if they were correctly sorted

The total 36 - 2 - 6 = 28 rewards correctness and penalizes both errors and delay. options.misconception: Wrongly grants the agent complete state information.

options.text: Partially observable, stochastic, static, continuous.
options.misconception: Mistakes unseen changes for random action outcomes.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, static, discrete.
options.misconception: Ignores both passing time and continuous positions.

options.text: Partially observable, deterministic, dynamic, continuous.

The layout changes while the agent deliberates, so it is dynamic. Positions range over a continuum, so it is continuous. Each competing option flips one of these four properties and therefore misdescribes the task.

questions.stem: With 0 and 11 as the stated parameters, on a four-connected grid an agent starts at (0, 0) and must reach a goal at (11, 3). Each unit step costs 1 and no obstacles are present. What is the Manhattan-distance heuristic value at the starting state? Give the exact answer, using only the information above.

Uses the area of the rectangle instead of step distance
Counts only the larger coordinate displacement

questions.explanation: Manhattan distance adds the absolute coordinate differences: |11 - 0| + |3 - 0| = 11 + 3 = 14. Because there are no diagonal moves, this is also the exact optimal path cost. Multiplying coordinates, dropping one step, or keeping only the larger displacement each fails to sum both coordinate gaps and so understates the distance.

questions.stem: With 9 and 2 as the stated parameters, a two-ply game tree has a MAX root with two MIN children. The first MIN child has leaves 9 and 2; the second MIN child has leaves 1 and 3. Under minimax with both players choosing optimally, what value is backed up to the root?

options.misconception: Swaps the roles of MAX and MIN at the two levels
Assumes MAX gets to pick a leaf directly
Assumes MIN chooses at the root

questions.explanation: Minimax backs up values from the leaves. Each MIN child takes the smaller of its leaves, giving 2 and 1. The MAX root then takes the larger of those, 2. Taking maxima at the MIN level swaps the players, while taking a global maximum or minimum ignores the alternating levels entirely, so each of those answers misapplies the recurrence.

questions.stem: For informed search, illustration 1842: a heuristic h satisfies h(n) <= h*(n) for every state n, where h*(n) is the true optimal cost from n to a goal. Which property does h necessarily have? Work through it carefully, based on the details given.

options.text: Consistent: it obeys the triangle inequality on every arc.
options.misconception: Wrongly names the stronger arcwise condition.

options.text: Monotone: its value never decreases along a path.
options.misconception: Wrongly states the opposite of the usual monotonicity direction.

options.text: Optimal: it guarantees the best path without any search.
options.misconception: Wrongly claims a bound alone searches the space.

options.text: Admissible: it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

questions.explanation: The inequality h(n) <= h*(n) is exactly the definition of admissibility: the estimate never overestimates the remaining cost. questions.stem: Working from 0.17, 0.73, and 0.7, a disease has prevalence 0.17. A test detects it with sensitivity 0.73 when present and has specificity 0.7 when absent. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability, to four decimals, that this person actually has the disease?

Reports the prior probability of disease
Reports only the joint numerator, unnormalized

The numerator alone is not a probability because it is unnormalized, and the sensitivity or the prior each ignore the false-positive contributions and the base rate, which is precisely the base-rate fallacy.

Computes the marginal probability of the child instead
Reports the conditional probability and ignores the parent

Reports the unnormalized numerator as if it were a posterior
Reports the prior and ignores the observed features

questions.stem: Read 7 and 9 with 8 first: in a Q-learning update, taking action a in state s yields an immediate reward of 7 and leads to state s'. Uses the first successor value instead of the maximum
Sums successor values instead of taking the maximum
